candidate.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — emergency response planning and incident coordination
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize ICS as a standardized, scalable incident-management structure that integrates command, coordination, resources, personnel, facilities, and communications during emergency response.

options.A: It creates separate command structures for each department so units can manage the incident independently.
options.B: It is a permanent organizational chart that replaces the hospital's routine leadership structure after the incident ends.
options.C: It is limited to police, fire, and emergency medical agencies and is not intended for private-sector organizations such as hospitals.
options.D: It provides a standardized, scalable incident-management structure that integrates command, coordination, personnel, resources, facilities, and communications.

candidate.rationale: FEMA describes the Incident Command System as a standardized approach to command, control, and coordination of incident management. ICS provides a common organizational structure in which personnel from different organizations can work together and integrates procedures, personnel, equipment, facilities, and communications. NIMS principles are scalable, flexible, and adaptable and are used by government, nongovernmental, and private-sector organizations. Therefore D is correct. A contradicts the common coordinated structure, B incorrectly makes an incident-management structure permanent after the incident, and C incorrectly excludes private-sector organizations such as hospitals.
candidate.source_claim_supported: ICS is a standardized incident-management approach that integrates command, coordination, personnel, equipment/resources, facilities, and communications within a common structure; NIMS/ICS principles are scalable and applicable beyond public-safety agencies.
